Hey all

I discovered this site a little over a week ago, from the recommendation of a friend. I've been studying intently ever since, and believe I've got a pretty good grasp on the fundamental concepts. I quit out of work last December to try to learn to trade - I only wish I'd found this site back then!

I have picked up a lot of bad habits of the last 7 or 8 months. I am impulsive, impatient, and overconfident with my trading. I've been trading on demo, and half the time I think it's the reason I don't take my trades more seriously - there are no real consequences. At the same time, I'm not going anywhere near real cash until I can become consistent on a demo account.

I'm starting this journal in the hope that it will make me more methodical, and make me hold myself accountable to the stupid decisions I make when in front of MT4. I frequently find myself just clicking the mouse randomly through impatience, and then get increasingly frustrated when I start to lose trades, leading me to become over emotional and then trying to "chase" to get the cash back. If I have to post up a picture of each trade I take with attempted justification, hopefully it will make me think twice about what I am doing.

I've made some great trades, that I've planned, and waited for patiently, and many more horrific trades. The first trade of the day seems to set the tone - if I get a winner, I'm happy to be patient for the next trade. If I lose, I want revenge. I should just step away from the computer at times like this.

Also I'd just like to express my gratitude to IF and the community at large for marking this such a great place to learn.

Cheers Simon

Some attempted analysis - UJ M30.

The yellow line appears to be compression (although there are some small pockets remaining on LTF). Having just broken into it, I would expect price to make it to the other side. I would look for entries on a RT to either the source of the engulfs higher up, or the FTR formed recently. I'm not sure which one it will make it up to. I will monitor LTF for signs of reversal at these points.

Hey Smimon!! Welcome to RTM. I look forward to seeing your future post!

SyT

As price approached the FTR, I narrowed the supply zone at the top to M5. Price showed signs of wanting to go down on M1 (inverted pins) at the edge of the zone, so I took an entry shown with the arrow, with my stop above the zone.

I had to go out, so couldn't monitor the trade. When I came back, I found that price had moved sluggishly away from my entry, and had restested it, with no opposite engulf, so I moved my stop to B/E. I then got stopped out.

The approach to the zone wasn't great - demand areas were created as we went up, instead of CP'ing smoothly into it. I probably should have passed on this altogether.

sylntthunder wrote: Hey Smimon!! Welcome to RTM. I look forward to seeing your future post! SyT

Hey pal, thanks for the welcome. Ferrari by this time next year hopefully;-)

As a quick aside - I have a very bad case of "magpie" syndrome. I watch about 6 charts, mark off zones of interest, and then wait for an alert to go off. I then seem to forget what I was doing, and start clicking aimlessly through my other charts, only to return 1h later and find the trade went off as I thought it would, without me! Another bad habit I've picked up over these last months.

With any luck, recognising and verbalising these issues will help me to focus in on addressing them.

EDIT: excuse me for waffling on, but thought I'd post this here instead of adding a new reply. Another thing I need to learn to do is relax a bit. I have been putting in upwards of 14 hours some days, studying, staring at charts, and generally getting worked up. As I'm sure we all know, sometimes you reach a point where the amount of effort you are putting into something starts to become counter productive. By taking a few hours downtime to read a book, play a game, hang out with friends, quality time with the significant other - even though I may feel like I am "losing out" on time I could be studying, the benefits from the more relaxed frame of mind far outweigh the small amount of extra info I could cram into an already frazzled brain during this time.

I want be trading to be stress free and relaxed. As long as I'm putting in at least 8 hours a day, I think that's fine. 14 hours a day doesn't fall under my definition of "relaxed"

This is a trade I am currently monitoring. Last week, EURGBP reacted from a strong H4 FTR (lower green zone), creating a H1 demand zone (upper green zone). Price is compressed on the approach back down. When we get back to this area, I'd be looking to take a FTB entry, targeting the other side of the compression.

There is a nice QM level on M5 within the demand zone, which I'd be looking at for entries.

Ok, so it's looking like I was totally wrong on UJ. What I thought was compression, doesn't appear to have been, but I'm scratching my head currently as to what price reacted to so strongly inside an area where I can't see any clear demand. The level does line up with a strong supply level (shown), but I wouldn't call it "ignored" supply by any means.

There's still a chance this top could hold it down, but it's looking bullish to my (extremely untrained) eye. Any thoughts welcome.

M30

Edit: Studying UJ a bit more closely, I think I see where I went wrong. Looking at the zone of "ignored" supply from the previous chart on M15, what I can now see is that price turned bullish from the demand that engulfed this level. Although the demand wasn't clear on M30, I should have dropped down lower to get a better view. Is this the correct way of looking at it?

Post mortem of my EG trade. I got in just below the QM level that I highlighted, with my stop below the demand, just after GBP news went off at 09:30, which pushed it down to this level. I've quite often seen news moves push things into good levels, where they subsequently turn.

This is the trade on M1. It actually got to over 3R off the initial surge, but I was looking much higher, and didn't move my stop to B/E (foolishly).

At 10:00, EUR news came out, and sunk EUR across the board like a stone, obliterating my trade.

Looking on H1, it's clear why this wasn't a good trade to try and hold for big profits. There was no engulf, and it was counter trend. I should have just taken the quick profit when it was available, or at the least, moved to B/E once it went clear.

Every single one of my trades goes into some profit - I don't seem to struggle identifying possible turning points, but I'm very poor at reading the "big picture" at the moment, knowing which trades I should hold, or just pass on altogether.

Never mind, still only week 2 with this RTM material. Onwards...

Here's one that I did spot, but didn't have the confidence to take at the top, owing to a few failed trades today.

Last time UCAD was up at these levels, this H4 FL was the source of an engulf of an important daily SR line (purple dashed).

Looking inside the zone at M1, we see the following:

When price returned, we had the following reaction short. However, as I was marking up the chart, CAD news came out at 13:30. Price had been moved into the source of an engulf of a FL that had been keeping the price down for a while, and the result was explosive.

It then proceeded up into the H4 supply source of the engulf of the daily SR line, before falling away (currently).

This stuff is starting to make more sense now, my main problem is realising which lines are going to be the most significant ones, but I feel like it's starting to click.

a number of setups from the Asian session, and there's a good period of volatility until about 0930, meaning you don't have to sit around for hours waiting for your trades to play out. 1000 - 1230 is the absolute worst usually, the "boredom zone" as I call it.

I took this short on GU. I had actually marked out the FTR from the drop yesterday, but didn't take the trade. Price fell off it nicely, engulfing an important level, before a strong overnight RT took us all the way back up to supply, just below the SR line. I TT'd the first return to the line - I could have in fact waited for an RT, but it's not really my style. I could have actually let this one a bit further, but the GBP news at 0930 spiked into my TP for about 6 or 7R, so I can't complain.

The other trade I noticed setting up this morning was EG. Strong engulf of a SR line from yesterday's drop on EUR news, RT back up to source, showing some good compression at the line. The fact that it CP'd off the supply initially, before CP'ing back to it again put me off a little, and made me set my stop much wider than I should have done, fearing a FO.

This is M30 (to show the SR line origin - it was actually itself a reaction to a H4 FTR from some time back)

The trade is shown here on M5. This one was good for just over 3R. If I'd used a tighter stop, I could have pushed it closer to 5R. I took profit from this just shy of my original target, because I'd reached my goal for the day, and it was close enough.

I also took a UJ long, which didn't work out, but I still managed to get out for about 1.5R before it went through my original entry.
I've spotted this juicy looking FTR on silver, which I've set up an email alert for, since it looks like it will be a good opportunity. Hopefully we'll see some nice CP back up towards it.

Here's a quick scalp I noticed on EG, but didn't take, owing to fear of losing my daily goal %age that I'd already reached. I'm not too bothered about this "fear" at present - it will go with increasing confidence in my ability to read price over time.

Reasons for entry marked on chart, stop and target shown with price labels. Good for around 6R.

Another quick scalp, GU short. Reaction from supply, FL eng, RT back to M1 supply, entry, target next FTR down, good for 4R ish.

Something seems to have clicked today, let's hope I can continue.

I took a limit on silver, and after an initial reaction, turned against me unfortunately. It then rose up to the higher SR slip line, where it's had a bit more of a strong reaction. I could have waited for confirmation from the top rather than taking a limit, but it looked like a good level. Win some, lose some I guess. I perhaps should have been aware of the upper SR line - it has some good history if I look back.

This does remind me actually of Infest's journal, where he mentions he won't take limits from "mid" levels such as this one, preferring to wait for confirmation. It's good advice.

NU on the other hand was an "edge" level. I took a TT right at the end of a big green candle, which was a bit scary, but I had confidence in the level - the drop from this source engulfed a number of important levels on the way down, so it seemed strong.

I'm currently sitting through a bit of a RT, but there's plenty of ignored demand for it to turn back down from - the ignored FTR (red box) in particular looks like a good level. The strength of the down move makes me think there is more to come - I might take an add if it gets back up to here.

Missed an excellent turning point on UJ today, largely through inexperience.

Analysing - we were at weekly supply of a weekly FTR.

One thing I seem to keep noticing (perhaps incorrectly), is that when you have a prominent level such as this, price turns not from the very top, but rather the first smaller TF FTR at the edge of that level.

Dropping to daily, we can see the first FTR:

Dropping to M30, we have a nice clean supply level at the top, that also lines up with a QM level (blue rect), and a SR line formed by the top of a previous, important FTR.

Fast forward to today, M15, and fireworks:

All easy enough to spot in hindsight, but I went blissfully unaware of it all happening today. I am certain all the top level traders on here were on this one from the top. Something for me to aspire to!

holding price up recently, so lots of nice FTRs created to be traded on any RTs. Hopefully by the time I get up tomorrow, we'll have seen some nice CP RTs into these levels. I'm not experienced enough to say which ones will produce good reactions yet, but I'll watch, learn, and try to get on.

Hi Smimon. I have just finished reading through your journal. You have a really good style of analysis. Keep it up!

Peds

Hey pal, thanks for stopping by. Yours was one of the most helpful journals I read through, I learned a load from it

Still a complete novice at present, but working hard to improve!

Hopefully I'll be able to add something myself to the community - I've noticed a few people check USDX or possible EURX for confluence on their setups - I went one step further some time back, and created currency indexes for all the other currencies (AUDX, CADX, CHFX, GBPX, JPYX, NZDX) according to their official trade weighted import/export figures against each other currency.

All of the setups work exactly the same on them - FTR, engulfs, FL etc. It really helps to give you more confidence in your trades, and when you get opposing setups occurring simultaneously (long USDX, short NZDX for instance) that's when the cross pairing really flies (the drop on NU yesterday for instance). I'll post up some charts of the currency indexes too along with how I use them.

Cheers

Ok, well typically, after a good day yesterday, I got massively overconfident. Such a problem for me - I stop doing the things which made me trade well the day before.

I tried to go long on EU, and the corresponding short on UCHF, failing to notice that both had turned at significant levels, and sellers were still in control on EU, buyers on UC.

Getting stopped out on both, but convinced I was still correct, but had just not spotted the FO level, I went in again - on both. And got stopped out again - on both. Good job I'm only on a demo account eh

My reasoning, H1 UCHF:

What I failed to spot:

So basically, the next important level below hadn't actually been engulfed, so sellers weren't still in control as I thought.

After 4 losing trades back to back, I'll make this a study day, to avoid making more emotional decisions, and probably more mistakes.

Key for me is being able to determine who is in control at any given time - buyers or sellers, then I know whether to look for entries long or short. If the last significant engulf was of a short level, then buyers are in control, and look for longs on RT. And vice versa. If we have just reacted to a strong level short however, with no engulf, then sellers in control until shown otherwise.

Obviously these levels exists on all TFs - buyers could be in control on M5, but overall sellers are in control in the H1/H4 picture.

Something for me to bear in mind.

I've traded pretty poorly today. I spent too much time on LTF, trying to be a scalping ninja, and lost sight of the big picture. I still managed to make a few good trades.

This on EA was a peach. Excuse the size of the chart, but I needed to get all the levels in - this is M30.

The drop from the level shown by the red zone engulfed 2 decent SR levels, and 2 strong FTRs. There had to be a ton of selling activity at this level. Additionally, the lows left from the rise up overnight looked very weak, so I fancy this one to reach my target below this.

I've got to learn to identify these peachy levels, and just ignore the rest. They're so profitable when they work out.

Quick example of a trade I took with confluence from the composite currency indexes.

I saw this setup on EN, the M5 supply that was the source of the engulf was clearly visible.

Before I take any trade, I like to check the corresponding index to make sure I'm not getting myself into trouble.

This was NZDX at the time. It's a composite made up of 5 currency pairings - you can see which ones go into it at the top right. The setup was mirrored on here, which gave me the confidence to take the trade.

At the same time, the following trade set up on NU - I missed this one however, because I had been watching the FTR above, which got taken out on the downwards surge. We went north off ignored supply/SR flip.

Looking inside that level on M1, we can see it was a lovely hook/cap on price, which got momo'd over.

These currency indexes are a blessing for me. I can spot setups forming on them, and get into position on the relevant cross pairing ahead of time. It never ceases to amaze me that the composite average chart of 5 different pairings behaves exactly the same as an individual pair. It just goes to show that the institutions like to take up views on currencies as a whole, and will move each individual pair into position ahead of when they are ready to make their move.

Just a quick update. Didn't really trade much today, what with NFP coming out. I saw a number of things at (what would under normal circumstances be) good levels for entry, a couple of minutes out. Too obvious - I figured the ITs weren't going to make it that easy, and I was pretty sure that things would then go exactly the other way, and they did.

I feel like the entries I've done well with this week are almost lucky as much as anything else at this point - I can justify to myself when the trade goes well why it worked. But then there are plenty of other times where I've identified what I believe to be a strong level, and it's completely wrong.

Still, I've only been on this RTM stuff a couple of weeks. Rome wasn't built in a day. My levels of understanding are still increasing daily, and I feel getting the knack for knowing the best levels is something that's going to come with time. I shall continue reading journals, and staring at my charts until my eyes go funny, and I'll get there sooner or later.

I'm still trying to be a bit too "cute" with my entries I feel - looking for really tight stops, to pump up the RR. There's nothing inherently wrong with it, and it's perfectly doable, I'm just not good enough yet!

I need to start paying more attention to compression also I feel, it's a very important piece of the puzzle, especially when it's present on HTF.

Cheers for now, have a good weekend anyone who is reading this

One more thing - I need to get my analysis straight. I'm spending too much time stuck in H1/M30 etc, but still missing the big picture. Analysis needs to start from the top down - M1/W1/D1/H4/H1.

The trades on which I've been completely incorrect whether buyers or sellers are in control have been because I haven't actually looked at a daily chart, beyond a perfunctory glance. There may have been some engulf on H1 or H4 signifying a potential reversal, but nothing on the daily to indicate the same. Of course, an H1/H4 engulf can be significant, but only if you know you're coming off a daily or weekly FTR.

Take NU for instance. It can clearly be seen on the daily chart, that the last move down engulfed a very strong daily FTR in the other direction. Where was the source of that engulf? Somewhere inside the D1 FL shown in red.

Dropping TF to H1, the engulfed D1 FTR is poking in from the left, and we can narrow down the source of the engulf to the H1 supply area shown.

Dropping even further into M1 to pinpoint the source of the move, we can see there is a lovely cap on price, with a little hook into supply right at the top.

Fast forward to this week...

There would have been a beautiful limit available there, with a 70 pip stop (10 pips = 1 point for me, so I guess most people would call this a 7 pip stop). This trade would be up over 20R by now. There was also a very nice re-entry available on a RT, had I actually realised what the previous top had come off!

I can see exactly how some guys on here take trades like this, the problem is I only manage to see them in hindsight at present, hah.

Lesson learned. Get my bearings on W1/D1 first, and work down from there.

Quick example of the type of analysis I'll be trying to do this week. After a big move, I'm looking left to see what was engulfed (if anything). If we engulfed any significant FLs/FTRs, I'll be marking them on the chart, but in a greyed out version of the normal zone colour, so I can clearly see on my chart what is going on. I'll then be marking any areas of interest from where it will be possible to take a trend continuation.

This is EU, M15. We can see on this screenshot that a H4 FTR got engulfed on the way down from the NFP drop on Friday. I've marked on the H4 FL above this drop (which doesn't look like a particularly strong area of supply), and the M1 source and M1 FTR from this move. I'll then wait for price to get into these areas (if it does) in the coming days and attempt to take shorts from these areas (since EU has been dropping like a stone for weeks now).

As a matter of interest, as I'm sure we all know USDX has been on a beast bull run these past few weeks. We're actually now coming up to a pretty prominent weekly FTR area (the zones highlighted are prominent hook FTR areas of supply on LTF). In my (thusfar) limited experience, I wouldn't be surprised to see some kind of significant reaction from these levels either this week or next.

I'll be monitoring for any significant signs of engulfs south on HTF.

Trying to be more methodical. When you see any FTR engulfed, the key thing to consider is - what levels did the engulfed FTR itself take out? Were they strong levels? So is the engulf of this FTR actually significant?

My friend called it "FTR Top Trumps", it's a good way of looking at it for me.

I spotted this engulf of an FTR on NU. This FTR was formed from the engulf of another strong FTR, so it implied that the move that engulfed it had some strength, and that the next FTR above was the destination.

I waited for the RT back to source, which was also a minor SR flip area, and entered, targeting the next level above. My entry could have been tighter, and I bailed on the trade slightly short of my target, but the key thing for me here was I saw this coming, traded it, and it played out exactly as I thought it would.

One issue I have currently is that when I've got a trade on, I focus so intently on it, that I tend to forget the bigger picture of what I'm supposed to be looking at. I'm sure it's something that will get better with time.

USDX had been moving steadily downwards to ignored S, the top of the previous swing high pre-NFP. It was bound to make a good SR level. Here it is - I should have been keeping an eye on this one.

The second that it hit this line, all USD pairs across the board surged in the relevant direction. UCHF, which has been looking particularly bullish for some time, was simultaneously at the FTR formed by the NFP surge on Friday. It should have been an obvious long for trend continuation, and we had a great reaction from the level.

There is also some good CP just a little higher.

What with focusing on my NU long, I forgot that I should really have been taking a short from the level that was my target for my long trade. Never mind, next time.

Trade on EG - was looking for longs, since H4 had been showing some engulfs north, and there is room to run until the next FTR above.

Price initially reacted off the SR flip, and spent a long time at the top before making its way back down. This led me to believe that most of the supply had gone, and price was going to come back down one more time to pick up liquidity before taking it out.

I entered too soon to be honest - I took a TT as soon as price hit the M5 demand zone above the flip. If I'd waited a little, price showed some good small engulfs north on M1, before coming back one final time, which could have resulted in a nice, safe entry with very tight stop. I tend to "fear" the opportunity is going to run away from me if I don't get on it, something I need to work on. FOMO - fear of missing out!

My initial plan was to hold for the next HTF supply/FTR above, but as usual I got a bit twitchy and took the points when they were on the table, about 3 or 4R.

I was on UJ from the post NFP top on Friday too, and foolishly quit out halfway down today's drop. Owing to my earlier analysis of what price has reacted to at the top, this could go quite a bit further. It would have been perfectly possible just to chase my stop at a safe distance. I'm not going to be too hard on myself at the moment, when consistently getting into winning trades becomes more routine than novelty, I'm sure I will be more calm.

Took a few other trades today, but got my analysis wrong, and managed to escape with just a small loss on most. The only one I got completely wrong and took a full stop on was a silver setup, which moved against me too quickly. Mid levels keep getting me in trouble at this stage. Still, I've stuck nearly 30% on my demo account since Friday all in all, so I can't be too disappointed (although strangely I am!). As long as I can keep making incremental progress, day by day, I'm happy.

Not much to show today, traded poorly. Lost my first couple of trades, which always then puts me into a bad frame of mind - instead of setting realistic TPs, I start trying to aim to get all my losings back, and more, from the trades that go into profit, which invariably doesn't work out. Had a decent short on EG, but held for an unrealistic target, and it came all the way back up on me. Thinking it would react to my entry, I doubled up, only to lose both.

I feel like I'm frustratingly close with this stuff, but I'm still battling my own impulsive nature and bad habits.

Looking at some of the journals of the associate level and above traders is both inspirational, and frustrating when I compare my own somewhat muddled trading. Although I'm sure no-one just picked this stuff up and became a flawless trading machine within a few weeks (or maybe they did!).

Got lost on the LTF a bit again today. Discipline is key. We'll get there.

Quick spot of analysis before bed.

JPYX is approaching a significant level - the daily FTR formed from the engulf of the lower SR line.

At the same time, GJ is approaching a very significant daily FTR.

Looking inside the FTR on LTF, I see the following on M1 at the edge - a clear, strong FTR. I've set a PO at this level, in the hope of hooking a big move. GJ also seems to be compressing into the level on H1.

Also, UJ is approaching a significant level itself. The FTR show here...

Was created following the engulf of this level from 2008.

Again, looking inside on M1, we see the following - a strong FTR level, with an SR flip. I'll also set a PO here.

GJ is somewhat further away than UJ currently, but a sudden drop in GBPX could easily push it down. It seems a few strong levels are lining up at the same time - I could be completely wrong of course, but it's worth a punt, since the RR could be good. We've got a bit of JPY news overnight, which could give it the push into these levels. I'll post up the result tomorrow... probably be a post mortem;-)

A much better day today, added about 40% to the demo account, but my brain is utter mush, so can't write things up right now. I've had a bit of an AHA with flag limits, and the DP within that causes the break.

Too many trades yesterday to post up, but I'll show the principle of some the better ones I took.

One of a couple of things I am now looking for is for a flag limit to form at a HTF supply or demand level (FTR/SR flip etc). At some point inside the FL, a decision will be taken to break out of the FL. The subsequent move should show some decent engulfs, and then I will trade the RT back to the DP to break the FL.

A picture is worth a thousand words, so here are a few examples...

AU yesterday

EJ yesterday

EJ actually made this entry even more certain, if we drop down to M1 to look inside the area when price RT'd back to the DP to break the flag

I took both of these trades yesterday, but I'll be honest - I ended up taking profit off them before my target, due to my lack of confidence at this stage. I'm happy at this stage to have identified and used a concrete, replicable method for entry on decent trades with really good RR.

Here's an EJ trade I am on currently.

H1 setup was as follows:

However, we don't want to just blindly trade any return to an ignored level - we want to see some signs on LTF that we are going to turn at this level. Dropping to M1 to inspect the zone where price had RT'd back to the ignored FTR...

Well, EJ didn't work out - I was up almost 5R, and let it come all the way back on me and wipe me out for B/E. I should take at least half off these bets when I can see it getting into trouble. It took off a treat though, I'm happy with my entry analysis, just my target was unrealistic. I still think we're headed up to where I originally targeted, but we need a deeper RT first. Edit: see lower analysis

Some other quick trade on CADJPY just now, as labelled on the chart (M1). This one was good for 5R in about 30 mins. I actually should have held firther, since there was no PA indicating a reversal - it could go on falling.

This seems such a simple setup to me now I'm learning, you can read price like a book and see what's going on.

In actual fact, the cause of my unrealistic target on EJ, was not being aware of the significance of the previous engulf of the lower FL, and what we had reacted to at the top. Since there was still room to run down to the base of the move, I should have been focusing on shorts on this pair primarily.
Silver - near carbon copy of CADJPY.

It's taking a while, but I'm slowly overcoming my "need" to be able to pick tops and bottoms. The easiest trades with the highest probability come after you let price tell you what it wants to do. "Needing" to get the top or bottom correct to the pip is purely ego talking. That's not to say it can't be done - I'm just not good enough yet, and it's not necessary to be highly profitable.

It's no good making a stellar trade by picking the top or bottom once, and then giving it all back again by being wrong the next 5 times.

And this is why we should always check the weekly/daily TFs for direction before entering and exiting our trades... yesterday's candle on CADJPY engulfed a strong daily FTR (the strength of it is indicated by the fact that it took out the opposing FTR). Looks like today's up move was merely to pick up some more sell orders higher up, at the SR flip. I could have held this one, down to the ignored weekly supply shown lower, for more like 20R than the 5R I took. We'll see if it makes it that far.

Just spotted this on NU - price reacted to an ignored H4 FTR at the top, and momo'd over an important H1 FTR on the way down. It strikes me as important since it was the source of the push beyond the previous highs.

It's a simple process, as outlined on my charts from yesterday.

Method 1: "Safe", very good RR

1. Identify HTF Suppy/Demand or SR Flip or FTR of Significance 2. Wait for price to hit the zone 3. Establish the limits of the significant flag that needs to be broken to indicate a reversal 4. Wait for break of FL (with additional engulfs preferentially) 5. Enter on RT to source of break of FL

Method 2: Riskier, but sometimes necessary because if price CPs into our zone, we're not going to have a clearly defined FL to trade the break of.

1. Identify HTF Suppy/Demand or SR Flip or FTR of Significance 2. Observe price CP'ing into zone 3. TT edge of zone

When trading any crosspair, it's important to consider whether it's moving in one direction solely because of the strength or weakness of only one of its constituents. ITs often like to play currencies as a whole to my knowledge, rather than focusing on individual pairs. The best trades come when one part is weak and the other part is strong, resulting in swift movements.

CJ and UJ obviously share JPY as a common component. Any strength in JPY will therefore push them lower. However, CAD and USD are almost opposing currencies -over 80% of the value of the trade-weighted CADX index comes from USDCAD. Therefore usually as USD moves up, CAD moves down, and vice versa.

For this reason, we can see that the only way CJ and UJ will both go down convincingly is in the event of significant JPY strength. If JPY remains neutral, then the sole driver of the pairs will be USD, meaning that if UJ starts going down in the face of JPY neutrality, then CJ will start going up.

Which is essentially what's happening to my 2 trades up the moment, see-sawing off each other. A strong kick from JPY will push them both down, but I've effectively bet 50% against myself.

A good way to look at things is in triplets of pairings. Let's say EURUSD is going down in HTF trend - we therefore know that USD is stronger than EUR. Let's also say however that GBPUSD is headed up in HTF trend. GBP is stronger than USD. Logic then dictates that the strongest moves should be coming short on EURGBP. USD is stronger than EUR, but GBP is stronger than USD, and so therefore far stronger than EUR.

This is of course all academic, and it's possible to trade the currency pairs perfectly well in isolation, but it's always worth bearing in mind so you not only don't bet against yourself, but also so that you can pick up on something that's really looking like it's going to run.

Quick something I knocked up to monitor my average position when adding to a trade in progress, and show me where multiplying my total lots by a factor of x will put my average position. It moves up and down as the bid price moves up and down. The idea is that I wait for a sufficiently deep retrace that I can double my lots (or whatever) and keep my average position behind a "safe" extreme - typically a FTR, the engulfing of which would mean I would consider the trade dead in the water.

Once a trade is in progress and you double (or whatever) up, you essentially go double or quits. You're either out for a lot more at your target, or you lose the lot at B/E at your new average position level if price reaches it.

It's a concept called "Space management" I found on another forum some time ago. The idea isn't new of course. If you're feeling really bold, and your trade has run almost all the way to target, you can do something silly like x10 your lots for the final stretch, "compressing" your space. You can also remove lots to a trade in progress if it looks like it's getting into trouble, putting some in the bank, and moving your average position further out, "expanding" your space, and giving yourself more room to survive a deep RT. If the RT ends up continuing back in your original trade direction, you can "compress" the space back again.

It's more suited for swing or position type trades I think, running over many hours, days, or even weeks, but you can still use it on a LTF trade, as I am attempting to do here.

Something I hope to master, is if I get on something that goes on a good run over several hours, is to "compress" up my space upon every successful retest and hold of freshly created FLs after engulfs.

Unfortunately all the fancy position management tools in the world can't guard against idiocy. I doubled up too soon, losing my position, instead of waiting for the retest of the FL. Oh well, live and learn... (slowly it seems).

Ok, so here's something I'm currently pondering. Below is a condensed chart of UJ, M15, with some important levels marked.

Bear with me, as I go through what I'm thinking.

First of all, an observation - I've noticed that quite often, when you have a HTF FTR, or S/D extreme in general, price will react to the first lower TF FTR formed after the initial move away from the extrme. Not only react to it, but almost like clockwork, you get a tiny FO into the LTF level that the first FTR formed off, and away it goes.

UJ has currently come short off such a level - the hollow box at the top is the first lower TF FTR at the edge of a prominent D1 FTR.

Here's the daily chart, and why I think it is important:

And here's M15 of that area, showing the level we've recently had a short reaction to:

Now, like good traders, we don't just dive in immediately, but we wait for an engulf of a significant opposing FTR to give us some idea that the move has got legs, and then enter on a RT.

Referring back to the topmost chart, just below this level we're currently having a long reaction to, is a level I've marked W1S. It was a weekly supply extreme, which in fact formed from the daily FTR we've now had a move short off.

The initial move down from the top engulfed both the FTR from the upwards engulf of this W1S, and also the source of the move that engulfed the W1S. After travelling a little further down, we've had a strong retrace off the level that was the source of the engulf of the short level I've marked "1st FTR" - this was the 1st large FTR formed after the top of the W1S when we fell away from it way back in 2007.

Now, to my mind, the level we are currently coming long off is less "significant" in the scheme of things. The W1S was a weekly supply extreme, and so presumably required a good shove to push through. We then took out this "shove" level from the first drop.

What I'm thinking is that price is now likely to RT back to the first new FTR formed from the recent drop (marked on the chart, also a QM level), which should then open the way up for a drop down to at least the level I've marked "Eng src of next FTR" - it being, as the name suggests, the source of the move which pushed through the next FTR in line from the down move in 2007. However, time and again, I've seen these seemingly "innocuous" levels actually turn into massive trend continuations.

I'm wondering - is it just down to my currently flawed understanding of the market that I get things like this wrong? Or am I just being far too ambitious in even trying to predict what level we're going to fall down to, given that the current level we've reacted long from hasn't actually been engulfed yet? I presume the concepts of PAZ apply on weekly and daily charts, just the same as they do on H4, H1, M30 etc, it's just that it takes a lot longer to play out.

I'm sure it's possible to rate the relative importance of each FTR on the scheme of things - whether it was a daily/weekly level, where it formed, what the move from that level took out, and thereby derive an understanding of where we think price is likely to go. I'm just perhaps not very good at it yet, and require more chart time and seeing things play out in order to get better at the analysis.

One last quick observation - we've currently had a small short move off a FTR that formed at the same level as the last upwards FTR before the recent high extreme. I've noticed that quite often these are also significant levels - in the same way that the first FTR after a move from an extreme, so can be the level that the last FTR of the upward (or downward) move formed at, when we revisit the other side of it.

I'd want to see the level beneath engulfed first however before I have any faith in this current move.

I know that we can just sit and wait for price to show us the way, but I'm also convinced that with sufficient experience in analysis, it's possible to make a decent prediction of what we think is going to be the likely end point of a RT, before price even gets there, allowing us to set limits ahead of time. Where are we likely to RT to, if we've formed a nice short move off a HTF FTR? A fresh H4 supply level formed near the edge. I've seen a lot of the time, that if you draw a line from the body close of the candle prior to the momo candle (the two taken together defining the S/D zone), it gives you a good idea of where price might bounce from, allowing you to hone in on any important LTF levels around the vicinity.

You can also drop down through the timeframes, H1, M30 etc, and repeat the same technique to find the H1/whatever fresh supply zones "inside" the H4 supply zone, narrowing the range of nice RT levels even further.

For me, there are only 2 things I need to take a trade: - a zone that could turn price, be it a FL, FTR, QM, whatever - a reason to enter the trade

Finding zones is what RTM is all about. The excellent analysis techniques provide us with the means to identify possible turning points ahead of time. We could just set POs, and trust that more will work than will not, which is no doubt a profitable way of trading provided you're getting at least 2 or 3R on your trades.

But if we really want to bump up our win %age, we need a good reason to enter the trade at the zone, merely apart from the fact that price has arrived there. What's a good reason? PA of course. We let the market tell us the intentions of the ITs.

What's a good type of PA to look out for? For me at least, it's the initial surge from a level that engs something significant, and then returns to source. That's where we enter.

I like to use D1/H4/H1 for my zones, and M15/M5 for my entry PA. Once you get used to spotting these types of trades, they're everywhere. Some may only make a small surge up to the next zone, some may keep going for much longer - that's when your HTF analysis comes into play.

To my mind though, I'm quite happy grabbing 3 or 4R off a good surge in 30 mins. If I want to hit the equivalent of 20R on a trade, I've got 2 options - leave it running for ages, and risk my HTF analysis being wrong, or if I'm confident in my win %age, rolling the profits of the first trade into a second. If I lose, then I'm just back to where I started for the day. If I win the second, that's getting on for some decent account gain, depending on your risk level.

I like to trade between 2 and 4% risk depending on how much I like the look of things. If I hit 3R off a 4% trade (12%), and then roll that into a second and do it again (12 x 3 = 36, plus the original 12 = 48%) then I've almost increased my account by 50% just off 2 single 3R trades, which can usually play out in an hour or less.

I've even written it down so I can see it in front of me - "3R, and then 3R, that's all you need".

Obviously you need to be quite consistent to get this to work well, which is why I use the two steps mentioned above. I'll just post a couple of quick examples so I can illustrate what I mean.

Some thoughts on pinpointing good bounce levels for POs with great RR. Expect to lose a few, but pull even a couple off, and you're quids in.

The key is confluence of levels as always, which help us to identify which supply/demand levels are the important ones. I don't trade AJ unfortunately, I just loaded it up for a quick peek ahead of the open of the Asian session, and saw this.

Here's the candle body line concept in action again. I first learned of this idea a while back, when I was still in the wilderness before RTM, from a great trader on another forum, who called the concept a "zero line" (or "z line" for short), because it's quite frequently the point where breakout traders will have their trades zeroed out by a RT after they've moved their stops to B/E, before their stops are hit and add fuel to the fire, and the move continues on its way.

We can't just use them blindly, there has to exist a confluence of factors to strengthen the decision.

And of course, obviously, they do just represent a place within a supply or demand zone. But they represent a great place for us to start narrowing down our search for pinpoint trades. I've seen price bounce off them almost to the pip so many times over the time I've been trading, that it would be foolish of me not to include them in my toolkit.

Why do they work? Most of the time, if you draw them in and drop timeframe, you'll find that what has been marked is actually some local SR which held price up or down for a while before a surge, or also quite often the edge of the last LTF FTR which get's momo'd over by a surge, which then becomes an ignored SD level. Both of these things we know are usually good for a bounce.

Here's a daily chart of NU, where I've marked in some z lines and shown where price reacted to them. You can find them on any timeframe, but obviously the higher timeframe ones are more probable for big bounces.

Here's today's NU surge and drop on LTF.

Sunday's always a good time to play around with some code. After falling afoul of losing sight of the big picture last week, I've been messing around with a good way to superimpose HTF S/D zones on top of each other, in a clear, easily visually identifiable manner. I was previously using outline boxes with borders of various thickness, but I quickly ended up with a confusing mess of lines on my chart.

As I'm sure anyone who has experimented with drawing rectangles on top of each other in MT4 knows, it's got an annoying habit of flipping colours of overlapping shapes, so that you end up with weird and wonderful shades, none of which was what you originally wanted. It's possible to apply a bitwise negation to a rectangle's colour before drawing it in order to counter this effect, but you still run into problems when one part of a rectangle overlaps another, and one part does not.

The only way I could reliably find to achieve the effect I was looking for was to convert the rectangle's price/time co-ordinates to x/y using the built in function, and then draw a rectangle label exactly on top of the original one. Rectangle labels do not suffer from the aforementioned colour flipping problem, but they are fixed in position - as you scroll the chart, they remain fixed in the same place. As such, you have to implement a timer function to redraw them every couple of hundred milliseconds in the correct position, which is a bit of a bodge (there is a lag effect as you scroll the chart quickly), but works. Also some other small caveats like making sure you sort your list of rectangles into descending order of timeframe (W1 then D1 then H4 etc) so that the correct drawing order is respected.

All a bit geeky, but I'm still a software developer at heart, and I always like trying to come up with creative solutions to work around the limitations of software. The end result is quite nice - here's a recent chart of GBPCHF, where we can see price hitting the nested H1/H4/D1/W1 supply zones, and falling off nicely.

Next up on the list is a way for me to quickly indicate which zones are engulf sources, and getting some good colours to indicate engulfed zones on various TFs. The more information I can assimilate from a single glance at a chart, the quicker I can make decisions about which direction to try and look for entries on LTF, and trade accordingly.

As an aside, this approach also lends itself quite nicely to a S/D radar, which will show me, once the zones are drawn, at a glance for all pairs I trade which ones are currently in tradeable zones.

Hey pal, thanks for stopping by.

I simply wait for an engulf of an important FL (making sure we've checked on M1 if it's real, or a fakeout), and then assume price is going to reach the other side of the PAZ down (or up) to the next important FL on whatever TF we're on. It's then a case of waiting through the RT after the engulf until it gets to a likely level, and entering. Even better is when it reaches the last possible level that it can react to before it has to continue on its way. If you've read your engulfs correctly, those are almost a guaranteed trade, and the depth of the RT opens up a ton of space to trade into. 2 PAZs might only be 10 pips apart, but when you've had a 50 pip RT after an engulf, you've got a nice trade.

Longer term bias doesn't necessarily matter for a single trade - a valid setup is a valid setup after all - but if we're coming off a daily or weekly level, in line with the HTF trend, then I am more likely to hold on to a trade and let it run as far as possible. This is something I need to work on more really - my UJ trade went much further, but I'm still finding my feet, so when I've got good profit on the table, I tend to bag it quickly. The confidence for longer holds will come with time.

With counter trend trades, I will take everything at the first target, no exceptions, and then look to reverse if possible - the target for one trade is often a great place to enter an opposing one. With trades that go with the long term trend, then it's up to your discretion whether you want to keep hold of it in the hope it will blast through a few more levels - you can always monitor PA and get out when it looks like you've had an important FL eng go against you.

Bear in mind too that PAZs exist on W1, D1, H4 etc etc. Which PAZ we've engulfed into on which timeframe is a good way to give ourselves a directional compass for our longer term bias.

Hope that helps in some way.

Personally, I only draw the lowest or highest edges of a bullish or bearish flag respectively, rather than a box around the whole thing, since it seems to me that these are the important edges, but I'm sure there's a reason why most of the academy students draw the entire box. There are tons of examples in my journal.

This is an example of one of the charts I trade from. These levels have just accumulated over time, I occasionally have to spring clean my charts to clean them up. There are probably more levels on here than I need, but I'm still in the process of refining my identification of which levels matter most.

i.imgur.com/EFkP3XO.png

I try to find only the important engulfed flags/FTRs, and nothing else. I find them by looking left, and seeing what engulfed what. The HTF engulfed flags (shown in grey with a red or green "tab" at the end) are more important, the LTF engulfed flags (greyish dark green or red) act as guidelines to how we're going to get from FTR to FTR.

I will use HTF initially to find the more prominent FLs/FTRs - but as soon as I've marked it on H4/D1/W1 whatever, I drop on to M1/M5, and extend the zone to the left until I find the actual FL it formed off.

In this way, I know straight away which are the more important flags I should be looking at. I'll use PAZ formed by FTRs corresponding to H1/H4/D1 FL engulfs as a directional guideline, and the LTF FLs as a way of tracking how I'm going to get there, and which level we're likely to RT from.

Sorry if this is a bit confusing, but it's quite hard to summarise in a few paragraphs a process that it's taken me 3 months of staring at charts about 10 hours a day to figure at. It's really all about just starting with the basic building blocks, the engulf and the FTR, and then applying it over and over again in your chart history, until it's become second nature. I must have marked up a 1000 different places on various charts at one point or another. Sometimes if I'm bored, I just scroll back to 2009 or another random year, and start making on where I think the important levels are, and then scroll forward in time to see if I was right. Alternatively, just find somewhere a massive move originated from, draw a horizontal line from the top/bottom, and then scroll back until you find the place it started from, and see if you can figure out why.

The place where a strong decision was made to engulf an important FL can also be an important level in its own right, provided it's relatively close to the FTR (on the relevant timeframe). In my opinion, FTB to any level where there are large amount of untested orders is valid for a PO. Remember, all this FL/FTR analysis is merely an enhancement to basic Supply/Demand trading, and it's to help us locate the levels on the charts where the unfilled orders are. If we see an engulf in the favour of the trade first, then great - we've got a confirmed trade. However even if we don't see this, there are still many levels where we can be reasonably sure of a big bounce - certainly enough to get some profit out of, and then leave the rest to run to see what happens. These I believe are called SAS trades - "scalp and see". You'll probably never get 100% trade success with this method, but you can still take plenty of profit, and avoid taking any full stop out in most cases if you manage the trade properly.

We knew there were significant amounts of buy orders in that FL, because of how it formed - after the engulf of an important opposing level. We also could see there had been a large surge from the level. We could also see that the extreme edge of the FL had not yet been tested. All of these were good reasons to expect a reaction.

The best way to manage these types of trades for me currently is to enter the order in 2 parts. Take some profit where you see the first likely trouble area, and then hold the rest as long as PA supports it.

Haha, no worries.

Go Tools --> Options and set the number of bars in history/chart to something 1,000,000 - the option isn't in the dropdown, but you can overtype it. You need to close and relaunch MT4 for this setting to get picked up correctly. i.imgur.com/c652DOJ.png

Next, press F2 to go to history centre, find the symbol you want on the left, and click download. This might take a while. Everything going well, all the history should then appear. However, the history handling in MT4 isn't the best. You might have to click download again, and get it to "recalculate all timeframes", or right click on the chart and hit "Refresh" if strange gaps appear in the data. Also a relaunch doesn't hurt. i.imgur.com/YZ8uvwe.png

Eventually, it settles down and should be ok.

A warning though - if you've got a number of charts open, having this many history bars can use a lot of memory, and MT4 can start bugging or crashing out. Gaps can randomly appear in the data, or it gets stuck on "Waiting for update" when you switch TF. A relaunch usually fixes this.

In the worst case, it will crash completely, with the "Metatrader has stopped working" windows dialog, Every time you relaunch, after 30 seconds it happens again. To clear this, you have to open, quickly close down all charts, close, relaunch with no charts open, and then it's fine.

1,000,000 seems to be about the sweet spot, I only get very occasional crashes with this. Any more, and it becomes almost unusable. I actually have a separate instance of MT4 with 5,000,000 bars so I can look back on M1 about a decade, which I just fire up when I need it, and then close down again.

Have fun;-)

The most common mistake I see on here (not to try and sound all high and mighty - I make plenty of my own!) is people simply drawing a line from a swing high/low, and then treating it as engulf. We've got to consider that every FTR forms as a reaction to some FL. Whenever you see a swing high or low, mark it with a horizontal line, and look left, however far back in time you have to go back, until you find the FL that caused it on LTF. Draw a box around the whole FL, and if the FTR didn't reach the very edge of those orders in the FL, then a FO is always possible.

A couple of examples immediately springs to mind from recent PA on UJ. Here's H4:

Both these levels looked like they'd been engulfed. But both of them were FOs of the apparent obvious levels. How could we have known this? Simple, by dropping down to LTF, and extending our rectangles further back in time to find the FL that caused them.

Here's the top one M5:

Here's the bottom one M5:

Now let's look at that H4 chart again:

Both apparent FTRs were caused from reactions to a FL, but we hadn't reached the extreme set of orders (very edge of the FL) in either of them. We can't treat a FTR as engulfed until the FL that caused the FTR is also engulfed too.

Both apparent FTRs were caused from reactions to a FL, but we hadn't reached the extreme set of orders (very edge of the FL) in either of them. We can't treat a FTR as engulfed until the FL that caused the FTR is also engulfed too.

You just need to look left (and possibly left again) and see if there is any obvious RBR or DBD that was formed after breaking a level, that price is reacting to. That is then the level that you look for the break of, not the swing itself. This way, you can avoid FOs, by being aware of where the actual edge of the important FL is. Sometimes you get a series of stacked FTRs all on top of a FL - this is then compression.

Sometimes the levels look insignificant, like the one on GU. But the market tells us it is important, because the last FTR into the top formed after bouncing from it. Therefore the break of this FL (also bearing in mind what we'd bounced from above) was significant.

My style of trading has changed somewhat over the last couple of weeks.

Back in the day, before RTM, I used to just try and trade pin bars for reversals. Obviously, without a deeper understanding of how to read price, this was hit and miss at best. Sometimes pins indicate rejection of price, sometimes they represent consumption of supply/demand before a move continues. Having the context in which to understand these is vital - and RTM gives us that context.

Now, I'm moving back towards PA-based trading, but combined with the experience gained by applying RTM techniques. The 2 main things I'm focusing on are surges in price, and signs of rejection on M1 after a engulf + RT - pins, inverted pins, signs of momentum fading.

PBs/IPBs immediately following a strong surge that breaks through a range are usually a great place to get a quick continuation. PBs/IPBs following an eng + RT are also a great place to take an entry, with a longer hold available. Just the pins by themselves aren't enough however - you need to have identified that the pins are occurring in a logical zone to turn price. Sometimes after an eng we get a shallow RT, sometimes a deep RT. PA gives me the clue as to whether we're going shallow or deep in these instances.

I like this style for 2 reasons - first, it's essentially confirmation trades only. No more guessing where price might turn, you simply wait for the market to tell you what's going on. Secondly, by sizing your position aggressively with a stop just above/below the pins (this results in a stop of 2 or 3 pips normally, I'll usually then remove the stop and manage the trade manually - it's possible to get stopped out by half a pip otherwise) you can hit 3 or 4R within the next 3 or 4 M1 bars, and if it really takes off, you can get 20R or more without too much trouble.

This style works best during the periods of highest volatility (0730 - 0930/1000 & 1330 -1630). The faster price moves around, the more exaggerated PA becomes, and the easier it is to read it. It's a highly aggressive style, definitely not suited for everyone, and you need to be able to tolerate high levels of risk and think quickly to pull it off.

I'm coding up a couple of alerting systems - one that goes off whenever a strong surge in price occurs which breaks through the range of at least 10 previous bars (arbitrary number, might adjust this), and one that goes off when we have a cluster of PBs/IPBs. They're not the kind of signals that you could feed into an EA - they're "look, something is potentially happening, open up the chart and analyse it, and see what's going on" signals. This means I can effectively monitor several charts without having to sit here staring at them. I can be playing a game, watching a movie, reading a book or whatever, and periodically something will bleep at me, and give me a heads up.

I'm entering the end of my learning phase now (at least, the learning phase required to go live - the learning never stops!), and I've realised it's quite possible to hit 10R daily off these sorts of setups if handled correctly, sometimes an awful lot more. There are probably about 10 or 20 tradeable setups across 6 charts every day. I'm back to 4% risk, and so I'll make it my aim to hit 40% daily for the next couple of weeks. If I can do that, I've truly convinced myself beyond a shadow of a doubt that I'm good enough to trade my real cash, and multiply it rapidly. 40% compounded twice is nearly 100%, so it'd be doubling an account every 2 days if I can pull it off. I'm sure that's not sustainable indefinitely - there simply aren't enough orders in the market beyond a point, but that's a nice problem to dream about having!

I'm almost never totally, hideously wrong with a decision any more, so I'm happy to trade without a stop using this method, jumping out at b/e on a RT if I've read price wrong and the trade goes against me. Worst case scenario - I take a big painful loss, but that's the risk you take with aggressive trading.

Hi All,

I too have been following the topic of 'finding the origins' for a few weeks now. And like Smimon said, there is gold in the first page of the FF thread. I review those charts often to remind myself of how the IT's think and play tricks.

I wanted to add that there are 2 other gems in the 'origin' story right here under our noses.

Go to the videos link: www.readthemarket.com/index.php/education/education-videos and watch the videos named "What's an engulf" and "The FTR Trade" at least 3 times. Listen to every word. For me, the light-bulb lit up the last time I watched those 2 videos.

Next, get to work identifying origins on the charts. Watch what happens when price comes back. There are only 2 options, engulf or respect. When you get an engulf, what happens next? When the level is respected, what happens next? I find that the M30 or H1 chart is often low enough to see the ITs plans in advance.

@Kossack - you don't need tick data for identifying origins. Check what IF does in the FTR trade video - he starts with weekly and drops to daily. Tick data is nice to have if you plan on basing your trades on M1 charts. But even then, I think you can often pinpoint the same entries on M1 by seeing between the lines of the candles. It all really boils down to your trading style.

And the concept of fractals is interesting too. Watching origins on a M30 chart provides the same signals (engulf/respected levels) as an M1 chart. There are just way more of them in M1. At the same time, your targets in M1 are closer to the origins. So, use M30 and swing trade or M1 and scalp, it is all the same. Engulfs, FL and Origins work the same in any time frame. At least that is how I see it today.

Well, at the risk of getting ahead of myself, I feel like I've finally turned the corner on live.

Going from demo to live was more of a massive leap than I thought it was going to be The intensity of the emotional battle can't be compared. But as a positive, the lessons you learn on live stick with you a lot more than anything on demo. Ultimately, demo doesn't matter, there are no real consequences to loss, other than damage to your ego. Worst comes to worst, you just press the "reset" button. There isn't that option on live, and you really have to start thinking a hell of a lot more about what you are doing.

The main thing I have learned really over the last few weeks - there are some areas on the chart, if you do your FTR analysis correctly, that it is basically impossible to lose from. Either price reacts to the zone as expected, and you profit, or price breaks the zone, but due to its importance and perhaps the number of stops outside the zone, a decent sized RT begins almost immediately, allowing you to average out of an initial bad entry. I have taken perhaps only one or two full losses in the last 2 weeks, and that was just from my own error in entering in a stupid place through impatience. Every other entry I've taken, I've been able to average out of it it went wrong - this means using no SL of course, but once you are confident that you're always going to get a chance to get out if the zone breaks (provided you always wait to enter at the most important levels), then it's not a problem.

Also - a zone is merely a place to look for important SR/flip lines which you can expect to turn price. A zone 30 pips wide - price cannot turn anywhere inside it, there are always 1 or 2 key SR/flip lines which are the places to look for reversal PA on M1. An important zone (FTR) is just a container for SR/flip lines, inside which you can expect them to have a much greater probability of bouncing price strongly.

Once you understand that price turns from within a few pips of a line inside a zone, and not just "somewhere" in the entire zone, you can then avoid even thinking about taking a trade until price reaches the line within the zone, and you see some M1 PA indicating that opposing orders are going in. In this way, all of the fake tops/bottoms the ITs create before price reaches the real turning point mean nothing to you, because you know price is not yet at the correct line, and you end up actually welcoming a huge LQ surge into your zone that stops dead at the line you have marked. When you see a huge momo candle stop dead on your important line in your important zone, and start to flicker a bit - you just know you can hit it. Even better if price makes an engulf before the LQ surge up to your line, since this is now almost certain to form a diamond.

There are 4 or 5 main "species" of these SR lines. In no particular order, they come from: - a QM from a previously important FL edge that was faked, before price continued (we call this a FOFLQM - a Faked-Out FL that provides a QM) - a standard QM - the flip from the last *important* small scale FL into the top/bottom before the reverse (even better if this came from a diamond reversal) - the top/bottom of a LQ push that broke an important level, and falls inside the resultant FTR (or even just outside for a FO) - support/resistance from a previously important high scale FL edge in history

Whenever you find an important FTR, there is always at least one of these types of SR line near the edge of it. Sometimes you even find multiple types lining up on the same spot, which is even better. Then all you need to do is watch the price approach, wait for price to hit the line, form some kind of rejection PA, and hit the thing. Even it it breaks, price is going to make a RT, so you just wait for the next M1 reversal PA to appear, and enter again, averaging out easily.

Just a quick rant/very basic lesson today.

I occasionally scan through journals of some newer members, and see the same error being made over and over again.

You cannot ever hope to analyse a chart properly, and find important levels, if all you are ever looking at is just the PA that fits on the current screen.

CONTEXT IS EVERYTHING. We must know where the important levels from the past were, so we know where they were engulfed, so we then know where the resultant important FTRs were formed.

This process begins on weekly, and works down to H4/H1 (or lower if you like). We find important levels, find where they were engulfed, and draw the FTR. This can end up forming a chain. In this way, we know where we are coming from, and where we are likely going to, on every scale from major down to minor. Without this road map of price direction, it is massively difficult to make informed decisions on trades.

It did occur to me as I posted the previous diagrams that this was a gross over-simplification of how the market actually works, and it was not my intent to state the above as an immutable law of the markets - but then, every lesson in the Markepedia is along the same lines.

The theory taught here on RTM is along the lines of "If the market was a perfect model, this is how it should behave". You then go on to realise there are layers and layers of subtlety and nuance on top of all the basic building blocks, the mastering of which is what takes 1000s of hours of chart time, and enables you to make the leap from "competent but inconsistent trader" into "consistent and highly profitable trader".

However, as over-simplifications go, I believe that my second diagram is a much more useful over-simplification than the first one, and if a beginner were to adhere religiously to one price model they would be better served by using this.

As you say, the market is an inherently complex entity. The only way we can begin to make sense of it is by having a set of rules which should hold true *most* of the time. We then have to learn under what conditions they might *not* hold true, by repeated application and study of when they failed, and trying to consider *why* they failed in terms of the behaviour of ITs creating liquidity to fill large positions.

Every scale has PAZ. We are either at the edges or in the middle of a PAZ on every single scale at any given time. We have a "where we are coming from" and "where we are probably headed to" in play on every scale at the same time. The smaller scale FTR and PAZ give us a "how we are going to get to the likely destination" in terms of our larger scale PAZ. Sometimes an engulf happens, which does not play out for days or weeks, until price has RT'd all the way back to the opposite side of the PAZ on the scale on which it formed. Sometimes price only makes a shallow RT. Sometimes you believe you've seen an engulf, but it turns out to be a FO only after a lot more price action has played out, and confirms it as such. Sometimes you have what appear to be opposing engulfs in play at the same time on the same scale. Sometimes new price action plays out which invalidates your previous assumption, and you must remain flexible enough to change your mind quickly - sticking to a flawed assumption in the face of conflicting evidence is a recipe for disaster.

Really, it can be an utter nightmare for a beginner to wrap their heads around as we know, which is why we must start from a simplified model, and extrapolate exceptions and nuances from that point.

As we know, the further you are from a PAZ edge on any given scale, the lower the probabilities that price is going to behave in a logically consistent manner. As you get closer and closer to the edges of a PAZ, and factor in how price approached, what engulfs are in play etc, then the probabilities of you being able to take a successful entry at a level increase greatly - the fuzziness begins to come more sharply into focus. The greater the scale of the PAZ edge, the sharper the focus and the higher the probability of a successful trade from the level.

Over time, one realises (or I did at least), that 99% of the time the best thing to do in the market is wait. Wait until price arrives at a level in the manner you expect, when as many pre-conditions of "is this trade likely to be successful" are met. Pre-conditions include, but not limited to: - is price moving away from a valid target? - is there a supporting engulf in play? - have we had a LTF engulf of FTA coming off a HTF level? - is this FTB to this level? - is this the deepest possible RT level on this scale? - can price FO this level, and if so, where can it FO to? - how did we approach the level? - what is the scale of this level? - is there any high volatility news approaching? - can I see any LTF rejection PA from this level to confirm opposing orders going in? - is there a confluence of important SR near MPL of this zone?

The list is large, and this list is probably not exhaustive, but only when all things are taken into account can you start hitting high win rates.

I've been live for around 3 or 4 months now (can't remember the exact date). I'm pretty broke, so have only been able to fund a micro account. In that time, I have blown the account 3 times, and had to redeposit funds.

Am I losing 75% of my trades? Far from it. I win around 80%, some days I don't even take a loss, but then I get offside badly on a single trade sequence, refuse to admit I am wrong, and get margin called. I'm probably now on my 5th or 6th cycle of "double, treble or even quadruple my account in a 2-3 week period with a 80%+ win rate, and then hand it all back again with one stupid trade sequence".

Naturally, this has to stop. It's absurd to win 80% of your trades, and then blow your account.

One of the main reasons I've been able to keep the win rate so high, has been not using a SL. By only entering at important larger levels, and keeping the big picture in mind, it's been possible to average out of 95% of my bad entries - but then there's that 5% that break, and never come back... Sometimes, price is just on an uber trend, and will blow through levels you could have sworn should have given a decent reaction with no more than a 5 pip flicker.

I believe that with more experience, I'd probably be able to understand when price is in this sort of mood, and step aside. But it's only been just over a year since I found RTM, and although I am good at this point, I am not that good. And I've got bills to pay, soon.

One plus that has come out of not using a SL, it that is has really sharpened up my analysis skills - I only try and trade zones where there was another obvious cluster nearby that could bounce and let me out if things went wrong. In the process of trading like this, I learned that a lot of the most profitable trades come not from trading a level directly, but from trading the FO of the level. I've also become extremely tuned in to M1 PA, and can recognise a reversal forming usually before the candle is even finished.

Put it this way - how many times does price respect a valid level, as expected? And how many times does it either FO, or engulf it but immediately begin to RT afterwards? I'd say the latter scenario happens about 4 times more often. When you think about it in terms of ITs needing LQ for their positions, they aren't going to get much when price makes a valid bounce from a very obvious FTR. When price breaks above (or below) and comes off some random cluster instead though? They'll get tons. And with time and experience, you can spot these seemingly "unimportant" clusters well ahead of time, and be ready.

Now let me preface this next section with the following - this is not a whine, or a rant, and I am fully responsible for my own decisions I've made. I am also eternally thankful to this community for teaching me what I need to know to make money out of the markets.

With that out of the way, there is one small issue I'd like to highlight about RTM, and member's journals - almost no-one is honest about how many they lose or posts up their losing trades more than once in a blue moon. (this goes for me too of course)

I think the reason for this is obvious - we're putting ourselves on public display in a community of our peers, and our own egos coupled with a desire to earn the respect of said peers means we generally only post up our trades when we are winning. It's fine, and it's natural.

However - this creates a pretty toxic false impression that everyone else except you is winning all the time. This leads you into thoughts of "What am I doing wrong? Why do I lose so many? What do they know that I don't?"

In truth, I have probably been good enough to make a ton of cash from the markets for 6 months now. But I have become obsessed with never taking a loss. Things like when IF posts up a screenshot of someone with 125 wins in a row doesn't help someone like me - I am competitive and a perfectionist, and I firmly believe that anything anyone else can do, I can do if I put my mind to it.

All of these weeks and months of trading with no SL, all the time, have been as a direct result of me going on an ego trip needing to never be wrong, and under the impression that it is possible to win every single trade, and that there are a bunch of "high level" people on the forum doing it day in, day out.

Shadowpit yesterday had the candour to admit that he loses 50% of his trades, for small risk - but losses nonetheless. Which directly led to me sitting here thinking "What the hell am I doing wiping out my account every 3 weeks, when all I just need to do is take a win or take a loss, and move on?"

I don't want to blow my own trumpet, but I am really good now at finding price turning points that react within 1-2 pips. If I were to just take these levels with a tight SL on M1 -a lot of the time I could be making 20R+ several times over the course of the day. What then does it matter if I lose 5 trades?

So anyway this is just a cathartic tirade, but the upshot of it is from next week, I will go back to using a SL, and take my profits when I get them, and the losses too, in the full knowledge that I will end up massively up on average if I just stick to my guns. It's going to be a bit of a learning curve again - I need to learn how to stay calm, and not become emotional after losing a few trades in a row, which was traditionally a big problem for me.

Another benefit to trading a large number of instruments - correlations. Think CADJPY is about to go long? Quickly check UCAD - is it at a level it could go short from? Great, take the trade. Is it in the middle of a PAZ? Probably better wait.

As discussed previously, individual instruments do not exist in a vacuum. The Fx market is driven by money flowing from one set of currencies into others. It is no coincidence that when an entire currency is about to make a turn, it's major and minors are usually all at significant levels at the same time. In this way we can also usually get a good guess at which directions large news announcements are going to go - 5-10 mins out from GBP news for example, go check the big picture on all GBP crosses, see if they are sat at important levels, or have just turned from important levels 30 mins ago etc.

If you're looking at a setup on an individual minor crosspair, and none of the other crosses for this currency are reflecting the same PA or are at good levels, then you should probably wait.

Certainly, it's just a single piece of information out of many that must be taken into consideration. But the engulf is one of our main weapons of determining how far a move can potentially go.

The theory being that there are key price levels in the market, as defined by important FTRs (amongst other things), that contain many orders, which are defended. Once those orders are removed, price is therefore free to travel to the next important cluster, or the edge of the next PAZ.

The confusion comes when you realise there are many more types of level price can make a valid bounce from, not just FTRs. In this way, an important FTR can appear to be engulfed, but in fact price has made a valid turn from another type of level. The more that price FOs, the more confusing this picture becomes, and the harder it is to know exactly how far we can hold a trade.

Higher highs and lower lows are by themselves somewhat meaningless unless viewed in the context of FTRs/PAZ. A higher high that was rejected from MPL of an important bearish FTR is in fact a reversal signal, not a continuation signal for instance.

Ideally, when we enter a trade, we want to see price engulf the nearest important level in our favour. This is then our cue to try and hold the trade further. The harder it is to define a valid engulf however, the harder it is to have confidence to understand where price may be headed next.

I then fit DPs on SR etc into the context of these FTRs.
