We then fit the IT tricks in and around these.

Example - GJ short I took today i.imgur.com/MyECRTi.png

After a while, it's just the same old tricks, over and over again. The key is to learn to recognise: - which levels are likely to get ignored/faked, and where they are going to fake into - which important FTRs are good to trade from the near the edge without them breaking

I prefer the first scenario personally, because then I am either trading a reversal from genuine FO, or I am trading the RT cycle after an eng of an important level which can be large sometimes. A valid reaction to a valid levels happens far less often than the combined amount of times a FO or eng + RT happens.

The second scenario is totally valid however, and works well a lot of the time. The key to recognising which FTR edges are more likely to work is to recognise the smaller scale structure near the edge, and where it is located in relation to the next significant orders. This comes largely from experience, but generally you want to see something on smaller scale that can be faked, and something for it to fake into. Remember the ITs can't generate much LQ from turning price at a massively obvious level - if you can see if that obviously, so can the rest of the world.

One of the biggest breakthroughs in my trading came recently when I started trying to "think like the ITs". When considering the trade of any level, I now first ask myself - how much LQ can the ITs generate at this level?

A lot of traders are a lot more S/D savvy than they used to be. A valid turn from an obvious valid level means the ITs aren't going to get too many of their orders filled for big positions.

Instead, when considering a level, it's always a good idea to look nearby, and see if there is a better level that price was turned just before, such as this example here in the PA that is developing from the move up on GN. No guarantees this will work here - but the presence of that swing low "hovering" above the QM gives a great low risk/high RR opportunity upon return.

Yes maknill, you are correct. I had it in my mind that is was a "rule" that price was not allowed to do a continuation FO when it was coming off a valid HTF level - I thought continuation engulfs (FO of minor level and continue) could occur only when there was a HTF engulf in favour of the move in play - but I guess this is not a rule after all

There is a fine balance to be struck between application of a strict price model to enable us to make reasonable assumptions and predictions of price movement, but also when to understand that these are not set in stone and that rules can be bent (or sometimes broken totally).

Imagine a world with no FOs... how easy would all this be

If any of you are anything like me, you probably have markup on your charts all the time, showing zones of interest, marking where engulfs occurred, etc. Indeed, I've even written a ton of indicators to help me out with this, including a FlagLimit indicator which allows FLs to be defined on multiple scales, finds if they have been engulfed or not, monitors them for price proximity/enter/engulf etc.

Since I like to adopt a currency based approach to my trading, I trade all USD and EUR crosses, in conjunction with 7 currency indexes (I don't trade CHF crosses just because the spread on most of them is terrible (apart from ECHF and UCHF) and because the index confluence doesn't work too well). This means I've got over 15 charts open across 2 instances of MT4, all with marked zones and alerts on them. At any given time, especially in times of high volatility in the markets, there are alerts going off every 2 minutes. You can have been waiting patiently for a setup, and watching price, and suddenly another 4 alerts go off, and your concentration is pulled all over the place. My head is a mess, my thinking is muddled.

I am also guilty of having a proximity alert to one of my zones go off, and then just thinking "I'll go stare at something else, and wait for the alert to go off that price has actually entered the zone before I decide whether to hit it or not". As a result, when price does enter the zone, I've not been paying attention, and I am out of tune with the approach, the speed of it, the way the candles are forming etc, and I tend to just make a rushed hasty decision to hit the level without a second thought. Sometimes it's fine if I've analysed the zone correctly, sometimes it goes instantly wrong as I've misjudged the strength of the move.

Also, whether you are aware of it or not, the second you place a single piece of markup on your charts, a single line, box, whatever - your thinking is influenced from that point forwards. Every time you look at that chart, you are starting with a single default assumption based on your markup, and everything subsequently is viewed through this lens. If your markup is valid and accurate - great; but if it's not, everything you try to trade from that point forwards will be biased towards being incorrect. Think - how many times have you drawn a zone, and then later in the day some more price action plays out, and you realised it was totally incorrect?

All of this is to say - less is more.

I've realised that the only thing holding me back from consistent success (my equity is up and down like a yo-yo at present) is my mental approach and organisation. I need a clear mind, need to be able to focus, need to be reading price clearly every time I sit down and not base my thinking on a load of assumptions I made 2 days ago.

To this end, I now only set alerts on my currency index charts (crosspairs don't usually make turns until the relevant currency index is at the correct level anyway), and at the start of every day, I wipe every single object off my charts. This cleaning of the charts has 2 benefits - it not only makes sure you are really reading what's going on with no previous assumptions, it also over time will dramatically improve your speed of analysis by eye, until you get to the point where you can just eyeball a chart and know pretty much what's going on in under 10 seconds, and where the next likely levels in play will be. I also now do not allow myself to use "zone entered" alerts - if I receive a proximity alert for a zone, i turn everything else off, and force myself to stare at that chart until the setup plays out.

You can glean a lot more information out of a naked chart than a chart with 43 boxes and lines all over it. Don't forget, the manner in which price is moving (surging, driving, compressing, flagging etc) is one of the biggest clues we have as to future intent, or whether what we think is an engulf is actually a FO. Yoy simple cannot see this piece of information clearly with clutter everywhere.

Yes, couldn't agree more.

Step 1 is to identify the repeating mental patterns which cause us to make bad decisions.

Step 2 is to then implement rules or working practices which give us a fighting chance of not making the same mistake again.

Step 3 is to not get mad at yourself if you fail, simply to calmly realise your mistake, and reset to try again.

A "favourite" of mine - I am bored waiting for price to reach a level I want to trade, so I start scalping silly midrange PA on M1 in times of low volatility (M1 PA is much tougher to read when the market is slow). I then lose 0.5%. Annoyed, I try to make it back quickly. I lose another 1%. Then I get more annoyed, and double down on my next scalp. Then I lose 4%. Before I know it, I'm 15% in the red, and trebling my lot size on stupid scalps trying to just "win it all back in one go". All started from one silly boredom scalp.

When we stare at charts for many hours, it is easy to zone out. These are the times of real danger, because your conscious mind is not fully focused on what you are doing, and you can quite easily end up doing strange things that you wouldn't normally have dreamed of doing. I'm learning to spot when my mind has started drifting, and this is my cue to take a break and refocus.

Also, if you have entered a trade based on a setup, and find yourself wanting to close it long before it gets to the target, there are 2 options - write down on a piece of paper the reasons why you entered and why you think you should hold it to TG, and every time you find yourself wanting to exit too soon, just read what you've written. The second option, and the one I prefer, is to take partial profit, and just walk away from the desk and come back hours later. Many of my best trades are overnight POs which have had 8 hours to move in my favour without me messing with them

Partial close is such a huge help. Have been doing it for quite some time now and works like charm with putting one at ease.

Another thing, setting up MT4 built-in emails alerts and setting up one's phone for push emails saves one from watching charts all day long and doing stupid stuff like scalping M1.... been there done that. It is extremely detrimental to one's psychology.

Learning and managing yourself is much more work than learning technical side of trading. That's where we start blaming all the teachers and mentors while the issue is within us not with them. TAKE RESPONSIBILITY.

Let's say we are coming north strongly out of a W1 FTR, showing a engulf north on the D1 chart, price then "engulfs" south but shoots away from the zone like a rocket - then by combining all pieces of information available to us, we can be pretty certain that it was a FO, not an engulf.

Conversely, if there was a W1 eng south in play, price had RT'd up to some D1 bearish FTR, not broken it, and had then come down and "engulfed" the level - then we can be more certain in this case that it was an engulf, and not a FO.

Each piece of information the market gives us must be understood in context of the larger scale moves that are going on, and also considering how price approaches the level, and how it moves away.

As a general rule of thumb, something which I attempt to differentiate is: - a) a FL that forms from the engulf of a valid FTR - b) a FL that forms from the engulf of where a retrace started from

In the scheme of things, a FL of type (a) is far more important than a FL of type (b).

Well, it's there on the chart really.

A bearish FTR has to engulf a bullish level south, make a RT north, and then *make lower lows*.

If price comes up north, RTs south, but then *does not make lower lows* and then goes on to *make higher highs*, then it cannot be a bearish FTR by definition. The swing high point is therefore *a place where a RT south started*, as opposed to *the edge of a bearish FTR*.

My trading method is focused on the highest probability events only.

A price reaction from just inside MPL of an important FTR, or an engulf of MPL and then quick RT, are very high probability events. It allows me to profit 90% of the time. I've had to steadily develop a range of mental hacks to keep me from doing stupid stuff as I've gone along.

As I've discussed, I devised a trading style whereby I would always enter with a SL based on an ATR multiple to give me wiggle room, and size my risk over this distance. The entry was always to be taken using a button on my LotCalc EA, which would calculate the position size automatically, and place the SL for me.

The stop was not supposed to be moved, the position was not supposed to be added to, I was to have a daily loss limit, and I even coded rules into my EA to this effect... but I moved my stops, and had an awful habit of popping open the Alt + T quick trade dialog and taking multiple "revenge" positions to try and average out of a bad entry, circumventing all the rules I'd coded. Unhelpfully, this averaging usually worked... but on the odd times I was 100% wrong on the big picture read, price would rip against me, and I would get margin called, wiping out most of the account. I lost count of the number of times this happened. Admittedly, a large part of this was inexperience in trying to enter from levels I'd misanalysed, but there's no point in wiping yourself out just because you're still not the finished article.

I did some research online, and find a way to code a C# app which intercepts the Alt + T keypress at a system level, and blocks it. No more quick trade panel. This method of circumventing my rules now being disabled, my EA is able to enforce the "no more than 1 entry", and daily loss limit rules I coded in. I also made my EA log the initial SL position when a trade is taken, and automatically detect when I've moved it, and put it right back again. This now forces me to wait until the best possible place to enter, when I can get my ATR stop behind the next level which can bounce, should the one I am entering from break.

I was also having some issues with the steadily increasing balance of my account causing me to become anxious, and affecting my decision making. So to counter this, I now never open the terminal window, so I have nothing more than a rough idea what is in my account and how much £ I have in open P/L, and have configured my EA to show me nothing except %age figures. % up/down on the day, % up/down current position, all open positions etc.

This way, every single trade is executed (as best as I can fool myself) the same regardless of whether I've got £100 or £100,000 in my account (I wish;-) )

Anecdotally - I lift weights at the gym a lot. I realised that after you've learned the correct training methods, getting an impressive physique is really 25% time in the gym, and 75% diet.

Trading follows a similar ratio for me. Once you've learned how to read a chart, it's 25% analysis skills, 75% learning to control yourself and not self-sabotage. Getting good at that 75% takes a lot of experience, and even some little hacks and tricks such as I just described.

Also key is to realise when you have enough analysis skills to spot the potential for good trades, but it's just your execution that is causing you to fail. At this stage, you are better served by settling on a style you prefer to take your entries and run your trades, and then just repeating it mindlessly for month after month. Only in this way will you start to see consistent improvement.

Constantly chopping and changing your approach, or always thinking you "just need to know a bit more information" and scanning the journals of 10 expert level traders (all of whom have years more experience than you) - will in the long run just hold you back from progressing as quickly as you might if you just pick a style and stick with it. Just realise when you are "good enough", and will be better served by more practise, rather than more reading.

Hey, thought I'd check in and journal where I'm currently at, in the interests of keeping myself honest.

Well, I'm still not a millionaire.

As mentioned previously, my natural temperament is really not suited for trading -overconfident, impulsive, impatient. So as such, curbing this is taking a very long time, one painful iterative step after another.

The good news - progress is being made. Every time I make a cock up, I learn a bit more about what I'm good at, and what doesn't suit my personality, and I am able to make steps to adjust and hopefully correct the problem.

I am currently, and have been for some time, extremely good at spotting high probability reaction levels in the market. This is without doubt my strongest area. It's the rest of the skillset around this that has been letting me down.

I've been "ego trading" for some time now. What's the ultimate goal of trading? Is it to have a high win rate, and stroke your ego? Or is to make money as quickly as possible, regardless of the method provided that it is effective?

By ego trading to avoid loss, instead of trading to win, I have been cutting winners short, and really making life hard for myself in terms of having to sustain a high win rate. And in fairness, I can usually hold up a 90% or greater win rate. But when you're only snatching 0.5R off most of these, you feel compelled to up your risk to compensate. Risk 10%, to make 5%, and hope you can keep winning 80-90%.

When it works, it's fine. When you start losing a few, it's very tough to handle. I usually go for 2 weeks without significant loss, and then have a bad day which knocks the wheels off everything.

So... first thing is I have to learn to accept loss. And I have to reduce my risk, and aim for at least 2R off every trade. Remember, you only to need to win 33% at 2R to break even, it's not a lot.

Second - I simply cannot be trusted to TT. You know how the banks' algos are designed to surge price around in such a manner as to stir up maximal emotion and excitement in the market participants, causing them to act impulsively and without due thought and planning? Well, they certainly work on me. Of course, knowing that more often than not price is just surging into a reversal makes it worse in many ways - as soon as I see a huge surge, all thought goes out the window, and I start looking to fade the thing. Often it works, but when it does not, instant pain. Unplanned trades caused by excitement, impatience.

To this end, my EA now only allows POs. I am to maximise profit from my skill in finding very high probability reaction levels, and in this way I will only be taking planned trades. I never have the patience to wait for PA anyway, so at least this way I am ensuring I get best price.

At this stage, it's tweaks, not a total overhaul. My live account is not large, but doubling it weekly has become commonplace. In the past, I would unfortunately hand it all back every so often in a disastrous day. Now, I have a daily loss limit in place which I can't break, but I've still had 3 losing days back to back this week, which hasn't happened for a very long time. First day wasn't too bad, second I wiped out within 30 minutes of sitting down trying to fade a surge, and by the third I'd gone to bits chasing stupid PA at stupid levels, taking ridiculous TTs just trying to win it back. We all know how that ends.

So I'm upbeat anyway, confident I will sort this out and find the constant account growth consistency which has been eluding me thus far.

In other news, I'm working on a really cool piece of software which finds very tightly correlated baskets of crosspairs, and allows you to generate synthetic instruments to use for confluence. It's not uncommon at present for me to be looking for 10-way confluence on a trade decision.

The market in general is in a very highly correlated state at present, owing to the large financial flows going on between oil, stock indexes, and a large number of currencies.

Here's a screenshot of the work in progress.

Dudu is no fan of RTM, that much is clear at this stage, but I wish him well with his preferred analysis style, if it's making him good, consistent money. That's all we're in this game for at the end of the day.

Personally, I love RTM-style analysis. Is it perfect? Is it a panacea? No, not at all. Especially since the markets seems to be getting harder and harder to read recently (or maybe that's just me). It does however remain a sound and effective model to form a basis for looking for levels.

When I want to take an entry, I want to do so from a level that has "orders" (I'm not sure this can be thought of in the literal sense, but it's a good analogy for referring to important buying/selling levels on the chart). A FL/FTR that was formed after taking out a key opposing level - well, it's just a very good place to look for orders. Of course FLs/FTRs themselves don't "move the market" - the only thing that moves the market is people actually hitting the market with active buying and selling.

I've been using this approach for over a year now, and know that it forms the nucleus of a very successful, accurate method of trading. There are of course many exceptions and nuances, which take a long time to learn, and even when you "know it all", you still face the even larger battle of controlling yourself and your emotions - a battle which I am still nowhere near winning.

When I fuck up, I know it's my own fault, and no-one else's. Sometimes I make a total misread, but most of the time I'm just self-sabotaging. There's nothing wrong with the RTM style, provided you realise it's not a set of literal rules which MUST BE OBEYED AT ALL TIMES. Nothing works like that in trading.

The reality is, you have to take some of this, some of that, put the pieces together. Which HTF levels are in play, the trend, style of movement, PA, FLs/FTRs, engulfs, key SR (PAZ boundary, QM etc), even a bit of volume profiling, and a huge amount of experience.

There are many ways to skin a cat. I like this method because it gives me precision to anticipate massive price turns within a few pips, if I do my homework correctly. I'm interested in RR, and % on the account. Number of pips gained, number of trades won etc are useless metrics. All that matters is the money going on your account, and the quicker the better

The end result is to get rich. However you get there is largely irrelevant. We're all going to have our preferred styles, and be extremely defensive about them, that's just human nature.

Buying/selling symmetry levels are just clear places on the chart where you can see heavy buying/selling took place in the past. Very often, price will make a reaction upon returning to them.

If you want to sell for instance, it makes sense to look for levels on the chart where you can see evidence of strong selling in the past.

A QM, if you think about it, is just buying/selling symmetry followed by a FO. The "real" orders go in, price then FOs to stop out those with early entries and get some more people going the wrong way, it reverses and an engulf occurs, and then price returns to the "real" level where the first orders went in.

As it happens, that level on CJ gave only a very small reaction, which was to be expected really given the strength of the up move.

You can't just blindly fade and take FTB to every old FL on every lower timeframe. You have to put everything together in terms of the bigger picture, and learn when it's best to step aside instead of trying to fade, or indeed look for the quick continuation instead.

It's always worth having a quick flick through all crosses belonging to a currency ahead of high volatility news, get a feel for what the currency in general is doing. Don't forget, news is not random, it's always leaked to those "in the know", who begin building positions ahead of it. This is what we can often read.

In this case, GU M15, price was coming south out of a decent HTF bear FTR, and showing signs of weakness in the 0900 and 0915 candles (doesn't look like many buyers, long wicks, closing bearish). It was a reasonable bet that it would drop a bit further off the news.

I shorted GU, and went long EG a few minutes ahead of the news. I closed both soon after, because my GBPX index hit a key demand level. Nice quick pips.

GU M1

EG M1

We have just made a higher high, price has not yet reached any kind of proper supply level, and so therefore a bounce from this FL was quite likely to end up as a continuation. Had I been thinking a bit more quickly, I would have stopped and reversed my positions, but it's hard to remain ice cool when news volatility is in the market.

Don't forget though, price making a very strong LTF surge against HTF trend, right up until 1 minute before the news, is usually a contrarian indicator. It is the ITs getting as many people going the wrong way as possible, to harvest the LQ.

Volume profiling is another tool I've started to make more use of recently. If I can see large amounts of activity at a particular price level, inside an important FL, that lines up with some important SR, it's almost a certainty price will react there.

Take this level for example (AUDNZD H1, but could be anything):

Initially, looks hard to spot a level

We draw a custom volume profile around the top part, and immediately a high volume node (HVN) is quite clear. Out of all the accumulation that occurred within this choppy region, these were the price levels which showed the most activity. I believe this is a result of the way the banks' algorithms work - they perhaps instruct them to fill a big order at a certain price, and as price chops around it, it keeps taking small bites until their position is filled. Normally, we wouldn't be able to see this by eye, but the presence of the HVN gives it away.

Now also if we look, there is a clear FL that was faked out, before the move continued. What appears to have happened here - a bull FL was engulfed, and a new bear FL was created, the top edge of this being the key price level. ITs then wanted to load up on positions for a bigger move south, and so price chopped around the area, faking the FL north, for some time, until their positions were filled and price dropped off strongly. The presence of the HVN on the same level as the FOFL (faked-out flag limit) gives us an A+ very accurate price reaction level.

One thing to note - this calculation isn't perfect. When calculating a composite index for let's s component is raised to the power of a certain weighting. I'm always playing with various new tools I've coded up to help me make better decisions on which crosspairs to hit. When you trade using 8 average currency indexes as your basis, you are essentially trading all 28 crosses in the market.

A big part of trading successfully intraday is the ability to be familiar with your chosen instruments, to hold the story of how the various higher timeframes are fitting together into a coherent map in your mind. The brain is only of limited capacity however, and whilst you might be able to do this for 4-8 instruments, you'd have to be an Einstein level genius to manage it for 28.

To confuse things further, moves of differing sizes are always happening simultaneously on different scales. GBPUSD might be the strongest pair in the market for the week, but chopping on the day, and actually the weakest over the last 2 hours. Again if you only trade a small number of instruments, this is easier to keep track of in your mental map, but when you trade the same small set of instruments every day you run the risk of just staring at hours of chop some days when all the big moves are elsewhere in the market.

I came close to a grand unified theory of tracking currency correlations a while back, which enabled me to trade baskets of 10 or more crosspairs from a single synthetic instrument, but ultimately had to abandon it, despite several times successfully predicting the daily move of 2/3 of the market. I was basically trading a brand new set of instruments and synthetic charts every single day, and just couldn't keep up with the ever changing nature of it.

So as it is, I have settled on using the 8 average currency indexes as my basis for all entries. I can just about manage to keep up with everything this way. My basic strategy is to fade nice approaches to key FTB levels, ideally as HTF trend continuations, but even against trend will yield some few pips 90% of the time or more.

Even this has its complications however. Let's say GBPX is surging long towards a level you want to fade - which crosses to hit? You have a choice of 7.

If you pick only one, you risk selecting the worst one of the bunch which goes nowhere, due to the other currency component not showing any strength against GBP in that moment, even as all the other crosses move as expected. It's actually amazing how often this seems to happen, sod's law I guess.

The safest idea is to hedge your bets across 2-3 crosses which are showing the most strength/weakness against GBP at that moment in time, since logically, these should be the ones which reflect the bounce in the most promising fashion.

To that end, I knocked up a simple tool yesterday which allows me to draw a box around an area of price on my currency index, and see currency & cross performance graphs for that section of time. As always, pictures are worth a thousand words, so I'll show a quick example.

This was GBPX M5 as we were coming up to London open on Friday morning. Price was moving strongly towards a key HTF FL, FTB. This is always especially nice to see 5-10 minutes out from 0800, since very often the volatility from London open gives you a nice move.

Which crosses to fade it against though? You can always do a visual inspection of the other 7 currency charts, but this is quite a lot to manage in the heat of the moment. So, using the new tool, I would have seen this:

This is a performance graph of the period of time encompassing the 6 or so M5 bars which comprised the surge into the level on GBPX. Using this, I now can very quickly see that USD, CHF and EUR were the 3 strongest currencies in the market during this time, and so the 3 trades to take would have been: short GU, short GCHF, long EG. I'd of course have wanted to make sure that these 3 were at some sort of semi-logical place for a price bounce to happen.

There is one drawback to this method however - sometimes when an entire currency makes a HTF turn, the money flows out of it into a different currency which right up until the turn was the weakest currency in the market. But you can't predict this reliably (or I've not figured out how to yet, I suspect you could use short-term correlations for a clue), and it's adding extra complication to the method. Often if you've zoned out during the day and an alert that you'd set earlier goes off, you only have 5 minutes to make a snap decision, so you want the process to be as simple as possible.

Anticipating a news setup using currency index confluence:

It's a safe bet to assume most economic announcements are always leaked. This usually presents us with good opportunities to predict the direction the news will go, since we understand the tricks the ITs like to play in order to get people offside.

Every week or two, GBP has 3 days in the week where medium importance economic announcements come out at 0930 GMT. Whilst these rarely produce huge moves, they always increase GBP volatility for 30-60 mins afterwards, and present nice opportunities for quick profit.

The general approach is: - check the currency index for the relevant currency. See where it is. Has it engulfed a level 30 mins earlier, and is making a RT? Is it sat at a strong level showing rejection PA 10-15 mins ahead? Is it making a straight line move into a key level? Is it mid-paz, but moving strongly already in direction of HTF trend? - check the other currency indexes to find the best opposing currency to hit it against. This can be either one which is itself at a key level and can bounce, or one that is already moving strongly in the correct direction as compared to the direction we want to trade GBP, with room to run - from the 2-3 crosspairs you have perhaps filtered down to, perform the same checks as on the indexes. Levels, PA etc - wait until 5-10 mins before the news to enter. Most of the time you can enter 10 seconds before the news hits. Ideally, you want to see a LTF surge going *against* the direction you think the news will go, right up until it hits. This is usually a trick to make people think the news is going to go the other way. Another type of very nice setup we can see, is price making an uninterrupted surge for 30 minutes right into the news, into a key level.

So, for today's 0930 GBP news, we start with GBPX M15

As we can see here, GBPX is currently in a range, held by 2 FLs above and below. The HTF trend is down, so it is more likely the lower one will break. However, with 15 mins to go before the news, GBPX was sat right at the bottom of the range, and had not broken it. In my experience, it is extremely unusual for price to be sat at a valid level, and for a news surge to suddenly break it *and keep going*. Much more likely, is that an engulf has already happened in the lead up to the news, and then the news continues the move; or the initial news stab breaks the level, but then price RTs sharply the other way, to complete the move at a later date. This chart favoured GBP going long. (remember, we're not necessarily looking for a huge move, just to ride the volatility for 5-10 mins after the news hits. We can use our understanding of the bigger picture to inform a decision as to whether it's worth trying for a longer hold or not)

I won't post all the other currency indexes, but the one that caught my eye at this time was USDX:

USD had what appeared to be a short term trend reversal day yesterday, unrelenting buying pressure. However, we had reacted to a key FL overnight, hit support, and then made a clean push deeper into it. Whilst you couldn't bet on this reversing the move short, it was an important level, and the 2TB offered the chance of secondary, smaller bounce. This chart supported USD selling off for a short period of time.

Combining the 2, we deduce that GU is a good pair to try and go long on for the news. So the next step is to look at the chart of GU itself.

This a section of an GU H1 chart.

What catches the eye is a decent DP, which was spiked through very quickly, circled (I believe this was FOMC last week that did this). There is a decent chance that orders were not filled at this level, so we can realistically expect some sort of bounce upon return. The slightly higher line is key SR from a PAZ boundary. Price was sat just above the lower line 10-15 mins out from the news.

So we now have 2 currency indexes and the cross itself supporting the possibility of a short-term long move from the news. We would not really expect a large move, because the HTF pictures on GBPX and USDX do not support it at this time. The final step is to examine M5/M15 PA for the candles leading up to 0930. Here is GU M5:

Circled, we can see price has surged down strongly (herd is now selling) and is showing nice M5 rejection PA from a place we anticipated in the period 0915-0925. Seeing this, I entered 10 minutes out from the news, keeping an eye on proceedings. Had price started to shoot up with just a few minutes to go, I most likely would have exited, since as mentioned this is usually a contrarian indicator. However, as it was, the 0925 candle, the last one before the news, closed bearish, which was enough confidence for me to hold into the release.

Finally M1 of how the trade played out:

On this timeframe, we can actually see a small FL just below the very obvious SR line. This made for a good initial target (and indeed, final target in this case), since most of the herd will be expecting price to reach this SR line, and turning price before it gets there represents a good opportunity for the ITs to confuse. The news itself gapped open slightly lower, before recovering strongly, and coming through for a nice quick 25 pips in 10 minutes.

Seems like a lot of work for 25 pips? Perhaps, but when you consider a) with enough time and experience, this entire mental process can be performed in under 60 seconds b) putting all of the factors together, we end up with a probability of being correct most likely in excess of 90%

then I believe it's worth it.

Although today, this move was small and against the larger picture, it was still extremely predictable, and using the method outlined above, on many other days with other news setups, there will be a lot more on the table.
